The subject vehicle is a preproduction Stellantis-owned development vehicle. Aptiv personnel were operating the vehicle for the purpose of ADAS development. 
The subject vehicle was northbound on [XXX] approaching [XXX] intending to turn left on to [XXX]. The other vehicle (south bound on [XXX]) collided with the subject vehicle. Airbags deployed in both vehicles. The circumstances of the collision and the details of the ADAS equipment which was engaged during the collision are still being determined.
The two occupants of the subject vehicle and the driver of the other vehicle were evaluated at the scene by EMS. No one was transported to a hospital from the scene. Both vehicles were towed away. Later, both subject vehicle occupants underwent a precautionary evaluation at a medical clinic and were released.

Based on the customer's statement, the subject vehicle was travelling at a speed of 50-60 MPH on [XXX] southbound near [XXX] at 12:30 PM (PST) with Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Centering (LCF) engaged. The driver was following a box truck driven by her fiancee. The customer further stated that the vehicle was traveling through a section of highway where a cement divider was close to the lane of travel and that the "wheel jerked". The vehicle struck the divider with the left rear wheel and the vehicle then crossed to the right side of the highway and struck a wall. The customer was unable to state in which direction the wheel had jerked. The customer stated that the vehicle was beeping but the driver was not looking at the dashboard when the incident was occurring. There were no airbags deployed, and the customer reportedly sustained minor injuries. The subject vehicle was reportedly towed from the scene.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on 3/25/2025. Carfax and repair records indicated the vehicle had recently been involved in a previous incident on 1/08/2025 where the inner and outer tie-rods were damaged. Repairs included an alignment and EyeSight camera recalibration. As related to this incident, there was accident damage to the rear left suspension, wheel, wheel opening garnish, and bumper cover. The front bumper cover, grille, and right headlight were also damaged.
[REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]
Based on the vehicle inspection and the data acquired, Subaru determined that there were no abnormalities with the ACC or LCF systems. The roadway was curving to the right, but the steering input was almost neutral [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]. LCF was not engaged and there were no abrupt steering changes left or right prior to initial impact [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]. The data indicated there was no driver steering input until after the first impact.

According to the customer's statement, the subject vehicle was traveling in a southbound direction of [XXX] in Norwalk, OH with the Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Centering (LCF) engaged. The ACC was set to 60 MPH. The customer further stated that he heard an audible warning "ding", the LCF deactivated, and the vehicle drove into a ditch. The side airbags deployed, the customer was transported to a hospital and the vehicle was towed from the scene.
An Ohio Traffic Crash Report indicated that the incident had occurred several miles from where the customer had indicated, on [XXX] southbound, which is a rural roadway rather than a highway. The road condition was noted as having snow cover. The time of the incident was noted as 1:20 AM.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on 4/28/2025. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]
Based on the vehicle inspection and the data acquired, Subaru determined that there were no abnormalities in the ACC or LCF systems. System data indicated that LCF had canceled due to the driver not holding the steering wheel. The customer acknowledged the audible warning. The EDR data indicated sudden hard braking was applied, and multiple steering inputs were made by the driver which resulted in a loss of control. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]

According to the customer's statement, the subject vehicle was travelling on [XXX] in Queen Anne, MD with Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Centering (LCF) engaged. The vehicle left the roadway and impacted a tree head-on. The customer indicated that she was wearing a seatbelt and that she was transported to the hospital with moderate injuries. Photographs provided by a 3rd party auction site indicated that no airbags deployed. Damage to the vehicle was not consistent with a head-on collision with a tree or the level of injury allegedly sustained by the customer. The customer indicated that the vehicle was not towed, however, it is unknown as the customer was the only person involved and was reportedly transported to the hospital.
[REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] The customer's allegation included AEB not engaging and airbag non-deployment. There was no allegation involving the operation of ACC or LCF.
The vehicle owner's manual states that Adaptive Cruise Control and the Lane Centering Functions are designed for use on expressways, freeways, toll roads, interstate highways and similar limited access roads. Subaru was not able to inspect or retrieve any data from the subject vehicle. It was sold through salvage auction on 4/22/2025, prior to the customer providing notice.

The customer was not alleging any defect with the vehicle.  According to the customer, the subject vehicle was proceeding westbound on [XXX] in Warrenville Heights, Ohio at 65 MPH when it was struck in the right-rear by another vehicle. During the standard accident questionnaire, the customer indicated that Adaptive Cruise Control and Lane Centering Function were both engaged at the time of collision.
The customer is not alleging any vehicle or system defect, and the purpose of the initial call was to compliment the vehicle performance in the incident and inquire about body shop post-repair information.
According to the Traffic Crash Report, the subject vehicle was traveling in the left-center lane when it was struck in the rear by a second vehicle. The second vehicle was traveling in the far left lane. The driver of the second vehicle stated that he lost control of the vehicle due to hydroplaning and struck the subject vehicle.

During the initial telephone conversation, the driver's mother stated that her daughter was driving the subject vehicle on [XXX] North with lane assist engaged at the time of the incident. She claimed that the Eyesight system malfunctioned and caused the vehicle's wheel/tire to contact the curb/divider. During a subsequent telephone conversation with the owner of the subject vehicle and driver during the alleged incident, the daughter stated she was driving the subject vehicle on [XXX] North at 55 MPH when the lane departure function failed causing contact with the divider which damaged one of the left tires.  As a result of the collision, the curtain airbags deployed and the vehicle was towed to a body shop in Mamaroneck, NY.  When asked, the driver stated that she had been using ACC and Lane Centering.  No injuries were alleged as a result of this incident.  
On August [XXX], Subaru reviewed the initial telematics data [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION].
A New York State Police Accident Report provided by the customer confirmed the date, approximate time, roadway, city, and state of the incident. The report also confirmed that the subject vehicle was traveling North on [XXX] when it failed to keep right, striking a concrete barrier which caused the airbag deployment. The report further indicates that the vehicle sustained a deflated driver side front tire and that the barrier did not sustain any damage. The vehicle was subsequently towed from the roadway.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on September [XXX], 2022. The vehicle was found to be in a repaired condition at the time of the inspection. EDR data retrieval from the Airbag Control Module was not possible as the module had been replaced and scrapped by the customer's repair facility. If any DTCs were recorded in the Eyesight Control Module, including system cancel codes, they had been cleared from the vehicle's Eyesight system by the repair facility prior to Subaru's opportunity to inspect the vehicle. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION]  Based on the results of the investigation and the data acquired, Subaru determined that there were no abnormalities with any vehicle system, including the ADAS-related systems.

The California Highway Patrol Traffic Crash Report (TCR) indicates that the driver of the subject vehicle was travelling on [XXX] at a stated speed of 70 MPH in the LH lane approaching the second vehicle (van) which was traveling south in the RH lane. According to the customer's statement to Subaru, the customer had just changed lanes from the RH lane into the LH lane to pass the slower moving traffic. The TCR states the driver of the van indicated he was travelling at a stated speed of 40-45 MPH in the RH lane in heavy traffic with approximately 10 slow moving vehicles directly in front. The TCR concludes, for unknown reasons, as the driver of the subject vehicle approached the rear of the van, the driver allowed the subject vehicle to unsafely veer to the right. This caused the front right of the subject vehicle to collide with the left rear of the van.  The driver of the subject vehicle caused the collision by driving the subject vehicle in violation of California Vehicle Code Section 22107, (unsafe turning movement). Due to the driver's failure to maintain a straight path of travel within the left-hand lane of [XXX], the driver allowed the subject vehicle to travel to the right into the right-hand lane and caused the collision with the van. As a precautionary measure, the driver of the subject vehicle was transported to a local hospital due to possible injury with complaint of pain to the neck and back. There was no reported injury noted regarding the front passenger of the subject vehicle.
Subaru inspected the subject vehicle on 11/09/2022. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] Based upon the results of the investigation and data acquired, Subaru found no abnormalities with any system that could have caused this crash.

The customer was not alleging any defect with the vehicle. According to the customer, the subject vehicle was proceeding at a speed of 70MPH on the [XXX] on June [XXX], 2022 with the Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Centering (LC) engaged when the vehicle struck a deer. [REDACTED, MAY CONTAIN CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION] The weather was described as clear and sunny. Due to the collision, the vehicle's frontal airbags deployed and the vehicle was towed from the scene. There were no reported injuries to either of the two vehicle occupants (driver and front passenger).
The Eyesight owner's manual states that the Eyesight system cannot detect animals and lists a deer as an example.

According to the customer's statement, the subject vehicle was travelling eastbound on [XXX] at 74 MPH with adaptive cruise control (ACC) and lane centering (LC) engaged when a large pickup truck in front slowed down and customer's braking was not sufficient to avoid a crash. Based on the customer's description, the rear passenger, who was laying down across the rear seat with a dog, received serious injuries to the upper torso and was transported to a hospital as a result of the crash.  The driver indicated she believes that the pickup truck was rolling at the time of collision as she does not remember seeing any brake lights. She also confirmed that pre-collision warnings did alert her and that she responded by applying the brakes.

raw.Narrative:
On April [XXX], 2025, Toyota received a call from the subject vehicle owner stating that The caller was involved in a single-vehicle accident while driving their Toyota Prius on Highway [XXX] near Trinidad, California. It was raining heavily and the lane assist system nudged the vehicle, causing it to hydroplane and spin off the road. The vehicle sustained damage and was towed from the scene. The caller wanted to report the incident to Toyota in case it was an issue with the lane assist system that could affect other drivers. The caller also stated that the cruise control was not engaged at the time of the incident. Based on the customer statement that cruise control was not involved, this allegation was judged not SGO reportable at that time. Toyota initiated an inspection of the subject vehicle based on the customer allegations. 
On June 3, 2025, Toyota completed review of a field report of the investigation of the subject vehicle, which included EDR, Vehicle Control History (VCH) and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD). The VCH and PCS Freeze Frame Data (PCS FFD) indicated that ADAS L2 was engaged in the recorded moments prior to the crash. The PCS FFD recording contains approximately 8 seconds of pre-crash data and images. From the PCS FFD, Toyota observed the following: Dynamic Radar Cruise Control (DRCC) and Lane Trace Assist (LTA) were engaged from the start of the recording until 3.1 seconds prior to the collision. At this time, these systems were disabled when the brake switch turned on. The vehicle was traveling approximately 71mph leading up to the collision. The steering angle varied from -4.5 deg at the beginning of the recording to 48 deg at 1.8 sec prior to the crash, after which the images show the subject vehicle veering off the right side of the roadway.

Subject Vehicle is a Lucid-owned vehicle used by Lucid employees and contract drivers to test and validate ADAS features under development by Lucid. The Subject Vehicle included Lucid "Highway Assist" (HWA) which is Level 2 ADAS technology under development by Lucid in collaboration with its suppliers. The HWA function combines lane-keeping and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), but is not yet available on vehicles that Lucid sells to the public. As a Level 2 technology, HWA requires the attention of the driver at all times and is not expected to avoid all accidents.
 
On 7/[XXX]/2022 at approximately 3:58 am, a contract test driver was driving a Lucid Air northbound on [XXX] at 70 MPH. The driver reported that he engaged HWA and subsequently fell asleep. Telemetered data confirms engagement of HWA and indicates that the driver imparted sufficient torque on the steering wheel to override HWA. When HWA is overridden, it no longer provides lane-keeping and ACC remains active. Approximately 15 seconds later, the vehicle drifted out of its lane and impacted its left side against the roadside barrier on the left side of the road. The driver awoke after the impact and brought the vehicle to a stop on the side of the freeway. Lucid roadside assistance was contacted to tow the vehicle. No airbags deployed. There were no other vehicles or people involved in this accident and the driver was not harmed.

On February [XXX], 2025, at approximately 9:21 p.m. PT, the subject vehicle was traveling straight with highway assist (HWA) engaged in the left lane. According to the telematics data from the vehicle, at 9:21:25 p.m. a notification via driver display for high curvature warning was activated due to the vehicle detecting a curve in the highway. The notification was on for almost 10 seconds. At 9:21:54 p.m., the driver overrode Highway Assist by applying a steering torque of 4.2Nm, which transitioned the vehicle into Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC). The driver notification was activated, which should have alerted the driver to the transition from HWA to ACC. The vehicle then proceeded in a forward path with minimal steering input (less than 1.6Nm) until accelerometer data shows the vehicle came into contact with an object at 9:22:15 p.m. PT. The vehicle then came to a full rest moments later. Rivian believes that the driver failing to take control of the vehicle after he cancelled HWA was the cause of the crash and neither vehicle systems nor performance were factors in the crash.

Rivian believes the driver falling asleep was the cause of the accident and the HWA system was not a factor.

Update: Rivian is still working with the Tennessee Highway Patrol (THP) and the local DA to gain access to the Rivian vehicle for further investigation and assessment. The condition of either vehicle involved remains unknown and many details are still unavailable. We have learned that the THP vehicle that was impacted was in pursuit, or about to be in pursuit, of a vehicle traveling the wrong way down the highway. It may not have been parked on the side of the road as initially believed. So, the pre-crash movement still remains unknown but there is potential for a very unusual maneuver such as a sudden U-turn on the highway, rapidly reentering the lanes of travel from the shoulder, a vehicle traveling the wrong way at high speed, etc. to have been a factor. The subject Rivian vehicle is an early VIN Gen 1 vehicle equipped with Highway Assist, not the Enhanced Highway Assist recently released to Gen 2 vehicles. The investigation is ongoing.

On March [XXX], 2025, at approximately 6:45 pm ET, the subject vehicle was traveling with Highway Assist (HWA) engaged at a speed of approximately 73 mph. At 6:45:30 PM there was a significant steering input from the driver that overrides HWA, which transitions the vehicle into Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC). The vehicle continued in ACC for approximately 1 second, while drifting out of the lane to the left, until accelerometer data shows the vehicle comes into contact with an object at 6:45:31 PM ET. The vehicle then comes to a full rest about 6 seconds later. 
Just over one hour later, at 8:04 pm ET, the customer called Rivian asking for information about long distance towing. Information was provided but a tow was not requested by the customer or arranged by Rivian and it is unknown if the vehicle was actually towed. The customer did not provide any additional information about the nature of the crash or make any allegations that the performance of the vehicle was a factor. Rivian believes that the driver failing to take control of the vehicle after they cancelled HWA was the cause of the crash and vehicle performance was not a factor.

Rivian reviewed the vehicle logs from the time of the alleged incident and was unable to identify an event matching this description. Rivian believes that at the time of the customers experience no ADAS features were actually engaged.

On October [XXX], 2023, at 2:35 p.m. PST, the subject vehicle was traveling north on [XXX] at approximately 75 mph with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature, Highway Assist (HWA), engaged. While traveling across an overpass at 2:35:18 p.m. PST, HWA disengaged because the subject vehicle moved out of its ODD as a result of insufficient highway markings.  At 2:35:18 p.m. PST, the driver received audio and visual alerts to take over the subject vehicle through in-vehicle messaging. The driver did not heed the warnings and the vehicle began to drift to the right, at which point Lane Keep Assist intervened and guided the vehicle back to the left to avoid crossing over the lane boundary. After this automatic vehicle intervention, the driver finally retook control of the wheel but overcorrected, steering the vehicle to the left until it left the roadway and impacted the side marker at 2:35:21 p.m. PST, causing minor damage to the subject vehicle.

On October [XXX], 2023, at 5 p.m. PST, the subject vehicle was being operated at low speeds in stop and go traffic, on a highway with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature Highway Assist (HWA) engaged. According to the driver, a vehicle to the right of the subject vehicle attempted to merge in front of the subject vehicle, underestimating the distance needed to complete the merger and the other vehicle crashed into the subject vehicle. The crash resulted in minor damage to the subject vehicle. The state of the other vehicle is unknown but believed to also have minor damage. Data indicates that the driver of the subject vehicle did not have hands on the wheel for approximately 45 seconds before the crash or at the time of impact. Data indicates that the vehicle did not malfunction and performed as designed in response to driver inputs.

Update: On January [XXX], 2024, at 10:33:20 a.m. PST, the subject vehicle was traveling south on [XXX] at 77 mph with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature, Highway Assist (HWA), engaged. 25 seconds later, at 10:33:45 a.m. the vehicle notified the driver through a message on the driver display that their lane was merging ahead. 19 seconds later, at 10:34:04 a.m. PST, after no intervention from the driver, HWA disengaged because the subject vehicle moved out of its ODD as a result of insufficient highway markings.  At that same time, 10:34:04 a.m., the driver received audio and visual alerts to take over control of the subject vehicle through in-vehicle messaging. At this time the system did not detect hands on the wheel. Less than one second later, at 10:34:05 a.m., the driver put their hands back on the wheel and retook control but input a significant steering angle while still at a high rate of speed (75.4 mph) that started a loss of control. This steering input was not a result of the HWA feature, but an overcorrection by the driver. Over the next nine seconds, from 10:34:05 to 10:34:14 a.m., the driver steered the vehicle to both the left and right trying to regain control, they also applied both the brake and accelerator pedals at various times, sometimes simultaneously, until the vehicle departed the roadway and impacted the side barrier at 10:34:14 a.m. PST, causing damage to the right side of the subject vehicle and deploying the side airbags.
While the Rivian was in Highway Assist (HWA), the driver unbuckled the seatbelt, which disengaged HWA.  The Rivian was under the drivers control with HWA disengaged when the crash occurred.

On June [XXX], 2024, at approximately 7:58 AM PT the subject vehicle was traveling with Rivians Level 2 ADAS feature, Highway Assist (HWA), engaged at a speed of approximately 82 mph. On August [XXX], 2024, at approximately 8:01 AM ET the subject vehicle was traveling with adaptive cruise control (ACC) engaged at a speed of approximately 76 mph. ACC is not a level 2 ADAS system, but Rivian is submitting this report because there was some uncertainty in the verbal complaint about whether the driver was allegedly using ACC or Highway Assist (HWA), which is a level 2 feature. The driver initially reported that they were using ACC, but the Rivian call center mistakenly assumed HWA was activated and noted it as such. However, vehicle telematics data demonstrates that HWA was not active during the crash or in the 30 seconds prior to this crash and that ACC was the system in use leading up to the crash.
The verbal report from the driver was difficult to understand but Rivians takeaway from the incident is that the vehicle was in the left lane with ACC activated when the lane ended. The driver admitted that they did not react to the lane ending in time and the vehicle impacted the center divider with the side of the vehicle. Damage to the vehicle is unknown but the customer reported that the airbags deployed and that the vehicle had to be towed.

On April 1, 2025, Ford's Customer Relationship Center spoke with the claimant, who alleged that he was in an accident several days ago.  The claimant did not specify the date of the incident, but claimed that the vehicle, a 2024 Lincoln Navigator, was towed to [XXX] Lincoln on March [XXX], 2025. The claimant alleged that he was driving the vehicle in town, with BlueCruise activated, when his car suddenly accelerated forward.  He claims he avoided colliding with the vehicle in front of him, hit a loading dock, and cracked the vehicle's radiator. The claimant clarified that he was not injured during the incident and there are no other reported injuries.
During a prior call with the Customer Relationship Center on March 21, 2025, the claimant mentioned he had installed aftermarket stereo equipment and that some factory components were disconnected when the equipment was installed.  Following a dealer inspection, a service technician confirmed that the aftermarket stereo equipment was causing numerous electrical issues and that factory components had been disconnected during its installation. Furthermore, the claimant admitted to previously hitting a pothole and a sapling tree, causing front-end damage. It remains unclear if this incident is related to the loading dock incident. On March [XXX], 2025, the customer reported issues with the headlights auto leveling to the ground, BlueCruise malfunctioning, and vehicle alignment. He attributed multiple accidents to these malfunctions.
Ford has confirmed that the vehicle is equipped with Co-Pilot 360 Drive 2.0, which includes Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Center Assist (LCA) and BlueCruise technology. At this point, Ford has not been able to identify any related L2 connected vehicle data and is still investigation whether these features were active at the time of the incident.  Ford has initiated communication with the claimant to gather more detail, including the location of the incident. BlueCruise can only be engaged and operated within the designed BlueCruise Zones.  The feature cannot be operated for off-highway use.

raw.Narrative: On April [XXX], 2025, a Tesla Model Y, operated by Ford personnel for evaluation purposes, was involved in a rear-end collision while using Autopilot/ Full Self Driving (FSD). The Tesla Model Y was exiting Highway [XXX] North onto [XXX] and continued in FSD as it merged onto [XXX]. As the Tesla Model Y was slowing down due to traffic flow, it was rear-ended by a Volkswagen ID.4. On [XXX], a Honda Accord (Vehicle 1) equipped with Lane Keeping Assist System (LKAS) and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) was traveling at a speed of 78 MPH in a 70 MPH zone. As it moved parallel to Vehicle 2, a 10-wheeler, the Accord's brake system unexpectedly activated, while simultaneously, the LKAS caused the steering wheel to jerk, redirecting the vehicle to the right. Neither vehicle needed to be towed and the driver of Vehicle 1 was able to drive to his destination. The following day, Vehicle 1 was considered a total loss. The incident was immediately reported by the driver of Vehicle 1 as he is an associate of American Honda who was driving a company vehicle. The incident was reported to Fleet Response, a company vehicle program. Fleet Response then communicated the details of the incident to American Honda's Product Regulatory Office for further investigation and action.

Hyundai reviewed the traffic report and deduced that HDA could not have been engaged during the incident. HDA is only available for approved highways such as federal interstates. Hyundai also reviewed the EDR report and confirmed the driver entered the turn with Smart Cruise Control ("SCC") engaged at a set speed of 80 mph. The accelerator pedal was depressed throughout the event. The brake pedal was never depressed. Lane Following Assist ("LFA") engagement could not be confirmed however, a manual steering maneuver was performed approximately 2 seconds prior to the incident and the ESC engaged, indicating a vehicle slip.  Hyundai deduced that the operator could have entered the turn at a high speed, realizing that the vehicle may not be able steer itself through the curve, and performed a significant steering maneuver in an attempt to center the vehicle within the lane, causing the vehicle to lose control. 
Hyundai notes that the HDA/LFA/SCC systems are not Level 2+ systems and are not designed nor marketed to provide complete "hands-free" driving to the operator. Drivers must be ready at all times with their hands on the wheel to insert themselves into a manual driving task. Hyundai has implemented driver attention warning systems that alert drivers up to 3 consecutive times if hands are not detected on the steering wheel for a brief period of time.

**9/[XXX]/2022 10-Day Update**
Kia inspected the subject 2022 EV6 vehicle on September [XXX], 2022 and downloaded the vehicles EDR data. Based upon a review of the data, the subject vehicle did not have Smart Cruise Control with Stop & Go (SCC w/ Stop & Go) engaged at least in the last 5 seconds prior to the crash.  In order for HDA to operate, SCC must be engaged.  The EDR data identifies the following:  1) Sign of the last accelerator input is 2.5 seconds prior to crash 2) the first sign of brake pedal input is at 1 second prior to crash 3) the vehicles FCA (Frontal Crash Avoidance) system started warning the driver from 1.6 seconds prior to crash all the way to point of crash and went through all 3 levels of FCA warning (Level 1 warning 1.6-1.4 seconds before crash, Level 2 warning 1.3-0.6 seconds before crash, and the last Level 3 0.5 seconds to point of crash.).
Based on the EDR data, the accident was not caused by a failure and/or disengagement of HDA.

*7/14/23: Monthly Update*
Kia received the ACU from the subject 2022MY Kia Sorento and downloaded the vehicle's EDR data.  The EDR data indicates that the incident did not occur during engagement of Level 2 ADAS.  The EDR data shows that the driver was applying the throttle via the accelerator pedal (44% throttle application). As a result, the driver was overriding the vehicle's ADAS functionality (i.e., Smart Cruise Control and Front Collision Avoidance) at the time of the incident.  Kia notes that the vehicle is designed with such override logic to give a driver's input priority over the ADAS features (e.g., perform emergency avoidance maneuvers, etc.)
In light of the above, Kia believes that this incident is no longer eligible for continued updates.

Customer contacted Kia Customer Care on October 31, 2023 to report that his 2024MY Kia K5 was involved in an accident.  Specifically, the customer reported that he was driving to work at 3:30a.m. at 75mph in the HOV lane with cruise control engaged.  Customer stated he felt the steering lift his arm and pull him to the left and then woke up and realized he had hit a wall.  The vehicle was towed to a Kia dealer from the scene.  Customer reported he cut his bottom left lip and chin (received stiches) and was taken to the hospital.  Customer wanted to know why the steering wheel pulled to the left.  
The subject Kia K5 is equipped with Highway Driving Assist (HDA). HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. The driver is responsible for controlling the vehicle for safe driving as HDA is not an autonomous driving system.  In addition, HDA may not be able to recognize all trac situations and may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system.  
Kia inspected the vehicle on November 29, 2023. Damage to the left front corner and steering wheel was identified.  In addition, it was noted that the driver was not wearing his seatbelt at the time of the crash as the drivers seatbelt pretensioner had fired in the stowed position.  It is likely that the unbelted driver may have caused damage to the steering wheel during the impact with center divider.  Kia attempted to download the EDR but could not do so due to damage to the OBD II connection.  A further attempt to back power the modules via the internal fuses was made but was also unsuccessful.  Kia requested the dealer to remove the ACU and send it to Kia America for further evaluation, but the dealer mistakenly sent the ECU instead of the ACU.  Kia is planning on making another attempt to download the EDR this week.  If that is not possible, the ACU will be removed so further analysis can be done at Kia America.            
Kia was originally informed of this incident in October 2023. However, due to an error by the agent taking the call, the wrong form/script was used and thus the incident was not properly routed to the Kia department responsible for SGO submissions.  During Kias TREAD review for Q4 2023, the case was identified and determined to satisfy the SGO requirements.  Kia is reviewing its internal processes and taking steps to ensure that this does not occur in the future.

Customer stated that she suffered bruises and friction burns from the airbags deploying and requested that Kia pay her vehicle loan and provide with a new vehicle.  
The subject Kia EV6 is equipped with HDA, LFA and SCC. HDA is a supplemental system that helps maintain a set distance and speed from the vehicle ahead when driving on a highway and helps keep the vehicle between lanes while driving. The driver is responsible for controlling the vehicle for safe driving as HDA is not an autonomous driving system.  In addition, HDA may not be able to recognize all traffic situations and may not detect possible collisions due to limitations of the system.  LFA is also a supplemental system that helps to detect lane markings and/or vehicles on the road, and assists the drivers steering to help keep the vehicle between lanes. LFA does not operate at all times and it is the responsibility of the driver to safely steer the vehicle and to maintain the vehicle in its lane.  
Kia has reached out to the customer and left several messages via phone and email in an effort to obtain authorization to retrieve the ACU and download the EDR data for its investigation into the customers allegations.  To date, the customer has not responded. As a result, Kia has no further information at this time.

9/13/2024 Update to 855-8237-2:
MBUSA conducted a scene and vehicle inspection on August 14, 2024, which included a physical examination of the vehicle. The subject vehicle was located in a salvage yard. The subject vehicle was left uncovered, exposing the vehicle to rain and other weather conditions (including heavy rains associated with Tropical Storm Debby). A significant amount of standing water was observed in both the driver and passenger footwells. As a result of this water damage to the subject vehicle, MBUSA was not able to establish a connection to the vehicle system diagnostics, control units, or EDR. 
A physical inspection of the braking and steering systems was subsequently performed. This inspection did not identify evidence of any steering or braking malfunction and the available information indicates both systems operated as intended at the time of the incident. The dashcam videos provided by the owner show the driver increasing the vehicles speed from 35mph at the start of the video to 46.5mph at the time of the crash. No audible warnings or steering wheel movement were observed in the driver-facing video. When DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist is active, the vehicle is designed to allow a driver to overrule and suppress the system by depressing the accelerator pedal. Based on the speed increase observed in the provided videos, it suggests that the system was not providing speed control to the subject vehicle prior to the incident.
Based on its investigation and review of the videos provided by the vehicle owner, MBUSA has concluded that that the vehicle operated as intended and that DISTRONIC with Active Steering Assist was likely not engaged during the 24-second period captured by the dashcam video recording and when the driver lost consciousness. MBUSA has concluded its investigation into this matter.

On July [XXX], 2024 Nissan learned of a news article reporting on July [XXX] of an accident involving an Ariya.  The incident reportedly took place at the intersection of [XXX] and [XXX] in Shelbyville, TN, both of which are not limited access highways. On July 31, 2024 Nissan determined that ProPilot Assist 1.0 was active ("hands-on" mode) within 30 seconds of the incident. Telematics data was last transmitted approximately 1,500 ft before the intersection. No crash notification was transmitted at the time of the incident.
Based on information in the news report, on Monday July [XXX], 2024, the driver of the Ariya was traveling north on [XXX] approaching an intersection with [XXX]. A tractor-trailer that was reportedly traveling west from [XXX] pulled out in front of the Nissan Ariya. According to the report the Ariya traveled underneath the trailer and continued approximately 100 yards before coming to a stop. The driver and passenger of the Ariya reportedly sustained fatal injuries. The tractor-trailer driver was reported not injured.
According to the police report, at approximately 6:15 p.m. on July [XXX], 2024, the Nissan Ariya was traveling north on [XXX] in the number two lane when a tractor trailer traveling west bound on [XXX] attempted to make a left-hand turn onto [XXX], traveling across the northbound lane. The police report states that the Nissan Ariya collided with the left rear side of the trailer and continued traveling north into the median.  According to the police report: the Ariya driver and passenger sustained fatal injuries and had to be extricated from the vehicle multiple airbags were deployed the passenger's seat belt use was "improper" the Ariya driver was belted and the tractor trailer driver was operating with a disqualified license.
Nissan obtained vehicle EDR from law enforcement. That data indicated that the speed at impact was 53.4 mph, with no pre-impact brake application. 
Nissan conducted a preliminary, non-destructive inspection on August 6, 2024. The vehicle had been stored in the open air and uncovered until August 3, 2024.  Various components were stored by the junkyard in an unidentified location and made available for inspection.  The vehicles condition is consistent with underride of the tractor trailer and extrication. 
The driver seatbelt was found buckled with the lap portion routed behind the seat, the pretensioner having activated and shoulder-belt webbing cut near the d-ring location. The passenger seatbelt was buckled, with both lap and shoulder belt pulled tight against the seat back, with the pretensioner having activated. 
Nissan was able to collect the vehicles ADAS control unit and Lane Camera assembly. Nissan is currently assessing whether it is possible to extract data, to the extent it exists, from these items.  
Nissan is continuing to gather information regarding this incident.
